study_material.title: Data Sufficiency - Complete Study Notes
study_material.introduction: Data sufficiency questions give a question plus two statements and ask whether the statements contain ENOUGH information to answer - you never compute the final answer. Judge each statement alone first, then together if needed.
learning_objectives: Apply the standard evaluation procedure (I alone, II alone, together)
Recognise when a statement narrows to a unique answer
Avoid actually solving when sufficiency is all that matters
Handle yes/no versus value questions correctly

concepts.heading: 1. The Standard Options
concepts.body: A) Statement I alone is sufficient. B) Statement II alone is sufficient. C) Either alone is sufficient. D) Both together are needed. E) Even together they are not sufficient. Read the option scheme given in the paper - orders vary.

concepts.heading: 2. The Procedure
concepts.body: Test I alone (ignore II completely). Test II alone (ignore I). Only if both fail alone, combine them. Discipline about 'ignoring the other statement' is the whole skill - leakage between statements is the classic error.

concepts.heading: 3. Value vs Yes/No Questions
concepts.body: For 'What is x?' the statement must pin down ONE value; x^2 = 16 alone is insufficient (x could be 4 or -4). For 'Is x even?' a statement is sufficient if it forces a definite yes OR a definite no - a definite no is still sufficient.

concepts.heading: 4. Sufficient does not mean True
concepts.body: You are judging information adequacy, not truth. Do not compute the answer - the moment you know it CAN be determined uniquely, stop.

formulas: I alone -> II alone -> combine (only if both fail)
Unique value = sufficient; multiple candidates = not
Definite yes OR definite no = sufficient for yes/no questions
shortcut_methods: Cover statement II with your hand while testing I
Hunt for counterexamples: two different answers consistent with a statement kill it
Watch for sign traps: squares, ratios and inequalities often hide two cases
common_mistakes: Letting statement II's information leak while testing I
Marking 'insufficient' because the answer is 'no' (a definite no IS sufficient)
Solving the problem fully and wasting time
study_material.summary: Evaluate each statement in isolation, combine only as a last resort, and remember that pinning down any definite answer - including 'no' - is sufficiency.
quick_revision_notes: Test I alone, II alone, then together

solved_examples.question: What is the value of x? I: x^2 = 16. II: x > 0.
solved_examples.step_by_step: I alone gives x = 4 or -4. II alone gives nothing specific. Together: x = 4.

solved_examples.question: What is A's age? I: A is 5 years older than B. II: B is 20 years old.
solved_examples.step_by_step: I relates A to B without numbers; II gives B only. Together A = 25.
solved_examples.shortcut: A relation plus an anchor value.

solved_examples.question: Is n even? I: n^2 is even. II: n + 1 is odd.
solved_examples.step_by_step: I: n^2 even forces n even. II: n + 1 odd forces n even. Each alone answers the question.
solved_examples.shortcut: Two independent proofs of the same fact.

solved_examples.question: What is the average of 5 numbers? I: Their sum is 200. II: The largest is 60.
solved_examples.step_by_step: Average = 200/5 = 40 from I alone. II adds nothing needed.
solved_examples.shortcut: Average needs only sum and count.

practice_questions.question: What is the cost of one apple? I: 12 apples cost Rs. 96. II: Apples are cheaper than mangoes.
How old is Ramesh? I: Ramesh is twice as old as Suresh. II: Suresh is 15.
practice_questions.explanation: The relation and the anchor are both required: 30.

practice_questions.question: Is x positive? I: x^3 > 0. II: |x| = x.
practice_questions.explanation: I: cube positive forces x > 0 - sufficient. II: |x| = x also holds at x = 0, so 'positive' is not settled - insufficient.

practice_questions.question: What is the area of the rectangle? I: Its perimeter is 28. II: Its length is 8.
practice_questions.explanation: Together: l = 8, b = 6, area 48. Neither alone fixes both dimensions.

practice_questions.question: Is m greater than n? I: m - n > 0. II: m/n > 1.
practice_questions.explanation: I directly says m > n. II fails for negatives: m = -4, n = -2 gives m/n = 2 > 1 but m < n.

practice_questions.question: What is x + y? I: 2x + 2y = 20. II: x = 3y.
practice_questions.explanation: I gives x + y = 10 directly - the individual values are not needed.

practice_questions.question: What is the two-digit number? I: The sum of its digits is 9. II: The number is divisible by 9.
What is the train's speed? I: It covers 240 km. II: The journey takes 4 hours.
practice_questions.explanation: Speed needs distance AND time: 60 km/h.

topic_test.title: Data Sufficiency - Topic Test
instructions: +1 for correct, -0.25 for wrong, 0 for unattempted.
Judge each statement alone before combining; never fully solve.

questions.question: What is b? I: a + b = 10. II: a = 4.
What is the perimeter of the square? I: Its side is 6 cm. II: Its area is 36 sq cm.
questions.explanation: Side comes from either statement (side lengths are positive), giving perimeter 24.

questions.question: Is k divisible by 6? I: k is divisible by 3. II: k is divisible by 2.
questions.explanation: Divisible by both 2 and 3 = divisible by 6. Neither alone settles it.

questions.question: What is the ratio of boys to girls in the class? I: There are 20 boys. II: Girls are 40% of the class.
questions.explanation: Girls 40% means boys 60%: ratio 3:2 from II alone. I alone gives no total.

questions.question: What is x? I: x is a prime number between 20 and 28. II: x is odd.
questions.explanation: The only prime between 20 and 28 is 23.

questions.question: Is the integer n a perfect square? I: n ends in 7. II: n > 100.
questions.explanation: No perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8 - so the answer is definitely no, which IS sufficient.

questions.question: What is the profit percent? I: The article was sold for Rs. 600. II: The cost price was Rs. 500.
questions.explanation: Profit% needs both SP and CP: 20%.

questions.question: How many children does Mr. Rao have? I: He has more than 2 children. II: He has fewer than 5 children.
questions.explanation: Together they allow 3 or 4 - not unique.
